name: Marco Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Marco. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and this is all confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager on the home farm at the Thornbury Estate. That's about 600 hectares of wheat, barley and beans, plus 250 beef cattle we finish in yards over winter, which means feeding them up to sale weight. My day starts in the cattle yards at six, then I'm planning field work on my laptop, running the team of three, and out on the sprayer or the combine depending on the season.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle, getting more grain from less fertiliser. I use AI every day to build fertiliser maps, so each part of a field gets exactly what it needs. What wears me out is money: estate pay is low, my partner Sofia rents a chair in a salon in Kelby, and last year I took a loan for a spraying drone to start a side business. So we've got about two weeks of savings and a three-hundred-a-month repayment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype? That would surprise me, but fine. I'd still use what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools that work are still worth having, and the rest was noise. At the estate office I'd show the land agent the fertiliser savings again. Online I'd say something like 'told you, it's about the boring bits'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a bit, because I've bet money on farms wanting more tech. The drone spraying still makes sense without big AI, but fewer farmers would get excited about it. And that loan doesn't care whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the drone business going and push hard to sign up ten farms this year. I'd keep using AI for the fertiliser maps, because it saves the estate about eight thousand a year. And I'd sit down with Sofia and make a strict budget until the loan's halfway paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm a numbers person, and right now the numbers are tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many farms do you need for the drone loan to work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About six regular customers covers the repayment. I've got four. The drone loan is three hundred a month whether I spray one field or fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sofia make of the drone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia thinks I'm a bit mad, but she also knows I don't sit still. She asked me to promise that if it's not paying by next autumn, I sell the drone. I promised.

think: I've **bet money** on farms wanting more tech.
The **drone loan** of three hundred a month doesn't care whether AI is hype.
do: Sign up **ten farms** for drone spraying this year.
Keep using AI for **fertiliser maps**, saving the estate eight thousand.

feel: A bit **uneasy**, because the numbers are tight.

fieldNote: His **side business loan** makes even a quiet scenario tense.

steps.text: Sign up ten farms for drone spraying this year
Keep building AI fertiliser maps for the estate's fields
Set a strict household budget with Sofia until the loan is half paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I'd bet on. And it's good news for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms that use these tools will do better, and I'd say it a lot. At the estate I'd pitch AI for field planning and grain sales. Online I'd post my drone results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one works out. The planning and buying on the estate is half of what I'd hand to AI, and I'm already the guy who does that. More farms would want drone spraying and someone to set up their AI tools, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up AI to handle grain marketing and input buying for the estate, which the land agent spends days on now. I'd grow the drone business to twelve farms and look at a second drone in year two. And I'd take on AI setup jobs for nearby farms on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Tired just thinking about it, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who loses out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the land agent's assistant, Helen, who does the buying paperwork. Helen would need to move into something else. The estate's a decent employer, so I think they'd find her something, but I can't promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got thin savings and a loan. Would you take on a second drone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the first one was fully booked for a season. I'm comfortable with risk, but I'm not stupid with it. A second drone is another loan, and Sofia would kill me.

steps.text: Set up AI for the estate's grain sales and input buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Then robots that can do field work as well as people by 2031. That's brutal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms need to move fast and governments need to help small ones keep up. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and online. I'd sound calmer than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a problem. By 2028 AGI would do the fertiliser maps and planning I sell, better and cheaper. By 2031 a robot could do my cattle work and spraying. My edge disappears, and I still owe money on a drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sell the drone while it's still worth something, and clear the loan. Then I'd apply to the robot companies that will need people to set up machines on farms, because I know both the farming and the tech. And I'd save as much as I can before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like being good at a game the day before they change the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling the drone feels like a big step back. Why so quick?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in two years a drone like mine will be worth half. Selling my spraying drone now is better than owing money on something nobody wants. I'd rather be clean and start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Sofia we're selling the drone, and that I'm going to work for the robot people. Sofia's salon is probably fine for a while, because people still want a person cutting their hair. She'd be our steady one.

say: I'd say farms must **move fast** and small ones need help.
I'd say it at the young farmers' club and online, sounding **calmer** than I feel.
think: By 2028 AGI does the **planning** I sell.
By 2031 robots do my **cattle work** and spraying, while I still owe on a drone.
do: **Sell the drone** and clear the loan.
Apply to **robot companies** as a farm setup specialist.
feel: **Anxious**, like being good at a game before the rules change.
S2.quote: Selling my spraying drone now is better than owing money on something nobody wants.
fieldNote: He acts **quickly and decisively**, cutting losses on the drone.
He sees his mix of **farming and tech** as his ticket into robot firms.
**Sofia's salon** becomes the household's steady income.

steps.text: Sell the spraying drone and pay off its loan
Apply to farm robot companies as a setup specialist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side. That's enough to make a proper move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready if farms start now. I'd keep posting my results and push the estate to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years lets me ride the drone business for a couple more years and then switch into robots before they arrive. If I'm the person running robot fleets for farms around here by 2034, I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the drone and pay it off by 2028. Then I'd turn the side business into a robot contracting firm, starting with one leased field robot. And I'd push the estate to bring in robots with me running them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit nervous about the money, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A robot contracting firm with thin savings sounds risky. How would you fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leasing and maybe a partner, someone like Tom Varga, who has a machinery business. I'd bring the farming and the customers, he'd bring the money. If it fails, I've still got my estate job, at least until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your team of three on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave and Lukas would probably move into running and checking the robots with me. Pete's close to retiring. I'd fight to keep them busy as long as there was work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can actually get it right. I'd tell farmers to start small and learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out well. I'd build up the drone business, save, and maybe buy into robots once they're proven. By 2039 I'd want to own a contracting business, not work for one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the drone, add a second one when the first is booked solid, and save a bit each month. I'd keep learning the AI tools as they come out. Around 2034 I'd start looking at robots to add to the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Excited. Ten years is a lot of time for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where it goes wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a big company comes in and does contracting for everyone at half the price. That's the real risk. Then I'd go and work for them, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger farmer starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a young farmer to learn the machines and keep their hands dirty too. Robots need someone who knows what a good crop looks like. That's the job that lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be caught with a loan and no time to change. What would help is cheap leasing for small contractors, so it's not just big companies that can afford robots. And some honest numbers from the robot makers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the cattle. Everyone talks about crops and data, but I'd like to know if a robot can tell when a steer is off his feed. A good stockman sees a sick steer before any sensor does.

headlineQuote: A good stockman sees a sick steer before any sensor does.
portrait: Marco, 27, is **farm manager** on an estate home farm with arable land and beef cattle.
He uses AI **every day** and runs a side drone spraying business on a loan.
With about **two weeks** of savings, his loan makes even calm scenarios tense.
He sees thinking AI as an **opportunity**, but fast AGI would make him sell the drone.
His plans grow toward **owning a robot contracting** business as warning time lengthens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd be caught with a **loan** and no time.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap leasing** for small contractors to afford robots.
